records.title: Couples Therapy for Intimate Partner Violence: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
records.journal: Journal of marital and family therapy
records.design: systematic review and meta-analysis (6 studies of 1,733 screened citations)
records.population_setting: couples in treatment for physical/situational IPV, mostly US clinical/research samples
records.key_finding: After screening 1,733 citations, only 6 studies met inclusion criteria for meta-analysis of couples therapy as a treatment for IPV; preliminary pooled data suggest couples therapy can be a viable treatment 'in select situations' but the evidence base is small and professionals remain cautious about risk of violent retaliation between partners.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Directly bears on the STOP RULE and P4 (joint work should stop where coercion/violence is suspected): the strongest available systematic review only supports conjoint work for a narrow, carefully selected subgroup (situational violence, not coercive control), with an evidence base too thin to generalize — supports T-PHE's caution but does not validate T-PHE's own untested programme.
records.evidence_level: systematic review / meta-analysis of controlled and quasi-experimental studies (small k=6)

records.title: Couples treatment for interpersonal violence: a review of outcome research literature and current clinical practices.
records.design: narrative review of outcome research and clinical practice
records.population_setting: IPV-affected couples in conjoint treatment settings, US clinical literature
records.key_finding: Concludes conjoint IPV treatment can be effective and safe only when embedded in a broader community response, with careful screening of couples for inclusion, modification of standard conjoint methods to promote safety, and ongoing safety assessment with contingency plans for escalation; a 'one-size-fits-all' approach is explicitly rejected given IPV typologies.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Supports P1/P4/bounded-authority-and-referral: names the exact structural conditions (screening, safety modification, ongoing reassessment, referral into a community system) that T-PHE's stop rule and six safeguards are trying to operationalize; T-PHE's stop rule is a stronger, single-threshold version of this literature's more graduated 'careful screening + contingency plan' model.
records.evidence_level: narrative review of experimental studies and clinical practice consensus

records.title: From scared to repaired: using an attachment-based perspective to understand situational couple violence.
records.journal: Journal of marital and family therapy
records.design: theoretical/clinical article (non-empirical)
records.population_setting: couples presenting for therapy with situational couple violence (SCV)
records.key_finding: Argues conjoint treatment can be appropriate for situational couple violence specifically (as distinct from coercive controlling violence), proposing an attachment-based safety plan and time-out strategy, while explicitly flagging cautions about appropriateness of couples counseling when violence is ongoing.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Complicates a blanket application of T-PHE's stop rule: reinforces that IPV typology (situational vs. coercive-controlling) matters for whether joint work is ever appropriate, which is exactly the distinction P4/the stop rule needs to operationalize but for which T-PHE (a conceptual synthesis, no assessment protocol specified) has not yet built a validated screening mechanism.

records.title: Women and men's use of coercive control in intimate partner violence.
records.design: cross-sectional comparative study, n=172 (85 men, 87 women), self-report (CTS2 + modified PMWI)
records.population_setting: community/convenience samples reporting on own and partner's IPV behavior
records.key_finding: Coercive control was associated with IPV similarly for men and women across three samples, and was predominantly reciprocal — both partners commonly reported both receiving and perpetrating controlling behaviors, regardless of physical-abuse status.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Complicates P4/the stop rule's implicit assumption of a clearly identifiable, typically unidirectional 'coercive control' pattern: measurement studies of general/community samples often find bidirectional reporting of controlling behavior, which is a known contested area in the field and a reason T-PHE needs an explicit, expert-informed assessment protocol rather than assuming coercive control is self-evidently detectable.

records.title: Psychometric Properties of the Coercion in Intimate Partner Relationships Scale.
records.design: instrument-development/validation study
records.population_setting: adult participants reporting on intimate relationships (validation sample)
records.key_finding: Reports on validity/reliability of the Demand, Threat, Surveillance, and Response-to-Demands subscales of the Coercion in Intimate Partner Relationships (CIPR) scale, developed because existing coercive-control measures had documented content-validity gaps (not capturing the full range of demand/threat/surveillance tactics).
records.relevance_to_tphe: Supports the STOP RULE / P4 operational need: shows a validated, multi-dimension instrument exists for identifying coercive control (demand, threat, surveillance), which T-PHE's 'confidential assessment' step would need to specify rather than leave undefined — a concrete gap in the current abstract.

records.title: Validation of the Coercive-Composite Abuse Scale (C-CAS) in an Australian sample of women experiencing intimate partner abuse.
records.design: instrument-development/validation study, n=854 adult women + qualitative survivor/expert feedback
records.population_setting: Australian women, community survey sample
records.key_finding: Developed and psychometrically tested a new self-report Coercive-Composite Abuse Scale (C-CAS) designed to capture severity, frequency and pattern of coercive control holistically, explicitly because prior measures showed 'limited understanding of these patterns of behaviour.'
records.relevance_to_tphe: Supports P2 (private channel makes concerns visible) and the stop rule's assessment step: a recent, patient/survivor-informed, psychometrically validated tool exists that T-PHE's confidential-assessment mechanism could adopt or cite, rather than relying on unstructured clinical judgment alone.

records.title: Coercive Control in the Courtroom: the Legal Abuse Scale (LAS).
records.design: instrument-development study, n=222 survivor-mothers, exploratory factor analysis + Rasch analysis
records.population_setting: US survivor-mothers involved in family law proceedings
records.key_finding: Developed a 14-item, two-subscale Legal Abuse Scale (LAS) to measure how family-court and legal processes can be misused by partners to continue coercive control post-separation.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Relevant to bounded authority and referral (P5) and repairability: illustrates that coercive control can persist through formal/legal systems after a couple separates, which is a downstream risk T-PHE's referral pathway and 'never resumes where coercive control is confirmed' rule should anticipate, especially for referral to legal/marital dissolution processes in a Thai/Muslim family-law context.

records.title: Development of a brief measure of intimate partner violence experiences: the Composite Abuse Scale (Revised)-Short Form (CASR-SF).
records.design: instrument-development study using pooled secondary data from 5 Canadian studies, n=6,278 adult women; international expert Delphi-style item rating
records.population_setting: Canadian adult women, pooled multi-study sample
records.key_finding: Developed a brief, validated 15-item short form of the Composite Abuse Scale, addressing the problem that most IPV measurement 'privileges physical violence, with poor assessment of other experiences,' which had led to underestimating the scope of IPV in populations.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Supports P2 (private channel makes concerns visible): a brief, low-burden, validated tool exists that could plausibly be embedded in a premarital private-channel step, but its short length is a known trade-off against fully capturing coercive-control experiences (see Evans 2016 below) — a design tension T-PHE has not addressed.
records.evidence_level: single psychometric development study (secondary data pooling)

records.title: Evaluating the Chinese Revised Controlling Behaviors Scale.
records.design: mixed-methods evaluation study, n=200 Chinese women survivors, in-depth interviews + ROC curve analysis
records.population_setting: Chinese women survivors of intimate partner violence
records.key_finding: Qualitative accounts of 91/200 women were consistent with Dutton and Goodman's coercive-control conceptualization; the Chinese Revised Controlling Behaviors Scale showed acceptable discriminative accuracy (reported via ROC/AUC) for identifying high-control relationships in a non-Western cultural sample.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Directly supports P3 (cultural tailoring helps only if culture cannot override consent/safety): demonstrates that Western coercive-control frameworks and instruments can be cross-culturally adapted and validated in an Asian setting, which is a relevant precedent for adapting assessment in the Thai Muslim/intercultural context T-PHE targets, while also showing this requires dedicated validation work, not an assumption of universality.

records.title: "Even 'Daily' is Not Enough": How Well Do We Measure Domestic Violence and Abuse?-A Think-Aloud Study of a Commonly Used Self-Report Scale.
records.design: qualitative think-aloud/cognitive interviewing study with a validated quantitative scale (Composite Abuse Scale)
records.population_setting: women with experience of domestic violence and abuse
records.key_finding: Think-aloud interviewing revealed systematic underreporting on a widely used, validated DVA scale, particularly for coercive control, threatening behavior, restrictions to freedom, and sexual abuse, driven by item-interpretation confusion, fear of answering truthfully, and reluctance to self-identify as abused.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Complicates P2/the private channel and the stop rule's reliance on self-report or brief screening to trigger assessment: even validated instruments substantially undercount coercive control specifically, meaning a premarital private-disclosure channel cannot be assumed reliable for detecting the exact pattern the stop rule needs to catch, without additional safeguards (trained interviewer, repeated contact, non-leading framing).

records.title: Examining strength at home couples to prevent intimate partner violence on a military installation: A randomized controlled trial.
records.journal: Journal of consulting and clinical psychology
records.design: randomized controlled trial, n=138 couples
records.population_setting: US military service members and partners on a military installation
records.key_finding: Service members randomized to the couples-based Strength at Home Couples (SAH-C) prevention program showed greater effect-size reductions than a comparison Supportive Prevention condition across physical, sexual, psychological, and specifically coercive-control IPV, plus greater reductions in suicidality; partner-reported effects were in the same direction but less robust.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Supports P1 (governance layer/decision control) with an important caveat: this is the strongest empirical evidence in this angle's search that a structured couple-based group prevention programme can reduce coercive-control IPV specifically — but it is a targeted prevention trial with built-in risk protocols in a screened population, not premarital joint education for a general population as T-PHE proposes, so it does not license extrapolation to T-PHE's context without similar screening infrastructure.

records.title: Screening for Intimate Partner Violence, Elder Abuse, and Abuse of Vulnerable Adults: Evidence Report and Systematic Review for the US Preventive Services Task Force.
records.design: systematic review commissioned for USPSTF (global-level guidance body), 30 included studies
records.population_setting: adults in healthcare settings, US and comparable settings
records.key_finding: Concludes screening instruments can accurately identify IPV in health care settings and that some interventions (e.g., counseling) following screening among women of reproductive age reduce IPV; harms of screening were assessed and found to be low, informing a USPSTF grade-B recommendation for reproductive-age women.
records.relevance_to_tphe: GLOBAL-level guidance supporting P5/the referral safeguard and the value of a structured screening-plus-response system: a USPSTF-commissioned systematic review is the highest-tier evidence in this record set that screening + appropriate referral (not joint treatment per se) is the evidence-supported public-health mechanism, which aligns with T-PHE's referral/accountability proposition more than with its joint-education component.
records.evidence_level: systematic review for a global/national guideline body (USPSTF)

records.title: A scoping review of intimate partner violence assistance programmes within health care settings.
records.design: scoping review, 43 included studies
records.population_setting: health care settings, multiple countries
records.key_finding: Of 43 studies across 9 categories of IPV assistance programmes (counselling/advocacy, safety planning, referral, resource provision, home visitation, case management, videos, provider cueing, system changes), programmes using a single active-assistance type combined with a counsellor/advocate reported positive results in 77.8% of studies, suggesting simpler, advocate-led interventions outperform complex bundled ones.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Supports P5 (referral quality = timeliness + accessibility + follow-through): evidence that referral/advocacy-based assistance (not joint couple treatment) is the intervention category with the most consistent positive results in healthcare-adjacent IPV response, reinforcing that T-PHE's referral safeguard, if built with a trained advocate/counsellor link, has stronger independent evidentiary support than the joint-education component itself.

records.title: Intimate partner violence: counseling, community resources, and legal issues for IPV victims and perpetrators.
records.design: clinical practice review
records.population_setting: primary/family care settings
records.key_finding: Describes RADAR (Remember to ask routinely, Ask directly in private, Document, Assess safety, Review options) as a structured clinical tool for identifying and responding to IPV, emphasizing private questioning, safety assessment (weapons, children, perpetrator risk), and advocacy-based referral requiring trained links to community resources.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Directly supports P2 (private channel) and P5 (bounded authority and referral): RADAR is a concrete, citable model for exactly the kind of confidential-assessment and referral pathway T-PHE's stop rule presupposes but does not itself specify; T-PHE could operationalize its own private-channel/referral safeguard by adapting a RADAR-like protocol rather than leaving the mechanism abstract.

records.title: Health care interventions for intimate partner violence: what women want.
records.design: qualitative interview study with pile-sort methodology, n=21 women
records.population_setting: US women with past or current IPV history
records.key_finding: Most women supported informational interventions and individual counseling; notably, only 9 of 17 who rated it felt couple's counseling was a good idea, with 7 explicitly reporting it was 'definitely not useful' — direct survivor preference data skeptical of couples-based response to IPV.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Complicates the case for any joint couple work where IPV is present, and supports dignity/consent and affected-person-visibility safeguards: this is direct, survivor-voiced evidence (not proxy/clinician opinion) that a substantial share of women with IPV history do not want couples counseling as a response — directly relevant to why T-PHE's stop rule treats joint work as something to halt rather than adapt when coercion is suspected.

records.title: Improving Provider Readiness for Intimate Partner Violence Screening.
records.design: pre-post quality improvement intervention study
records.population_setting: healthcare providers (nurses, physicians, social workers) at a US clinical site
records.key_finding: An EMR-integrated brief IPV screening tool plus provider education plus an automated resource/referral telephone system was associated with measured improvement in provider readiness to screen (assessed via the Domestic Violence Health Care Provider Survey Scale, pre/post t-test).
records.relevance_to_tphe: Supports P5 (referral timeliness/accessibility) and bounded authority: shows that referral quality and screening readiness are trainable, measurable provider-level competencies, underscoring that T-PHE's practitioner-led safeguards (epistemic humility, bounded authority) require analogous structured training and system infrastructure, not intention alone.
records.evidence_level: single pre-post quality-improvement study (no control group)

records.title: Implementing Trauma-Informed Partner Violence Assessment in Family Planning Clinics.
records.design: quasi-experimental single-group pretest-posttest + qualitative interviews (survey n=132 baseline, n=68 3-month retention; interviews n=35)
records.population_setting: women aged 18+ at two US family planning clinics
records.key_finding: A brief, trauma-informed, universal IPV/reproductive-coercion assessment and education intervention was implemented with 65% of women receiving at least one intervention element; the mixed-methods evaluation describes uptake and provider/patient experience of the assessment process.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Supports P2 (private channel visibility) and dignity/consent safeguards: demonstrates a real-world, trauma-informed implementation model for universal (not targeted) private assessment embedded in a routine service encounter, which is structurally analogous to what T-PHE's private-channel safeguard within premarital education would need to replicate, including its retention drop-off (52% at 3 months) as a caution about follow-through.
records.evidence_level: single quasi-experimental implementation study with qualitative component

records.title: Patient and provider barriers, facilitators, and implementation preferences of intimate partner violence perpetration screening.
records.design: qualitative study — patient interviews (n=10) and provider focus groups (n=29)
records.population_setting: US Veterans Health Administration patients and providers
records.key_finding: Identifies convergent and divergent patient/provider beliefs about barriers and facilitators to screening specifically for IPV perpetration (not just victimization), an area with a much thinner evidence base than victimization screening.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Relevant to P1 (decision control) and P4/stop-rule symmetry: highlights that screening for use of coercive control/violence (not only victimization) is understudied and operationally harder — a gap T-PHE's assessment mechanism would need to address for both partners, not only the presumed victim, especially given the coercive-control-reciprocity findings noted elsewhere in this record set (Robertson 2011).

records.title: Approaches to screening for intimate partner violence in health care settings: a randomized trial.
records.design: cluster randomized trial, n=2,602 eligible women across 6 clinical sites (emergency, family practice, women's health)
records.population_setting: English-speaking women aged 18-64 in Ontario, Canada healthcare settings
records.key_finding: Compared face-to-face interview, written self-completed questionnaire, and computerized screening for IPV to determine the optimal screening method in terms of accuracy, acceptability and completeness.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Supports P2 (private channel design): direct trial-level evidence on which screening modality (interview vs. self-report vs. computerized) women find acceptable and complete, directly informing how T-PHE's private/confidential channel for surfacing concerns should be designed rather than assumed to work in any format.

records.title: Factor structures for aggression and victimization among women who used aggression against male partners.
records.design: cross-sectional psychometric comparison study, n=412 women (African American, Latina, White) who had used physical aggression against a male partner
records.population_setting: US community sample of women who had recently used aggression against a male intimate partner
records.key_finding: Compared the factor structure and psychometric performance of three widely used IPV measures (CTS2, SES, PMWI) for assessing women's own perpetration versus victimization, finding the factor structure of women's perpetration differed from that of their victimization.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Complicates a simple unidirectional coercive-control model underlying the stop rule: shows that standard IPV instruments do not measure perpetration and victimization symmetrically even within the same person, reinforcing that any assessment tool T-PHE's stop rule relies on must be validated for the specific direction/role being assessed, not assumed generalizable.

gaps_noted: No PubMed-indexed study was found evaluating a couple-based premarital or pre-nikah education programme with an embedded coercive-control screening/stop-rule mechanism in a Muslim or Thai/Southeast Asian intercultural setting — the exact population T-PHE targets.

No PubMed-indexed study directly tests a 'stop rule' construct (halt joint work pending confidential assessment, never resume if coercive control is confirmed) as an explicit intervention design feature; the closest analogues (McCollum 2008, Schneider 2014, Karakurt 2016) describe screening/safety-modification practice recommendations rather than a validated stop/resume protocol.

Coercive-control measurement instruments identified (CIPR, C-CAS, LAS, C-CBS-R, CASR-SF) are validated predominantly in Western (US, Australian, Canadian) or Chinese-community samples; only one (Tiwari 2015, Chinese sample) offers a non-Western cross-cultural precedent, and none has been validated for premarital screening specifically (all are post-hoc/retrospective abuse measures, not prospective risk-of-future-coercion tools).

Evidence on screening/assessing male perpetration (rather than victimization) is comparatively sparse (Portnoy 2020), which matters for T-PHE's bidirectional/decision-control framing (P1) where either partner could be at risk.

No cost-effectiveness, implementation-fidelity, or long-term (multi-year) outcome data were found for any couple-based IPV-adjacent intervention in this angle's search; the strongest RCT (Taft 2024) is a targeted secondary-prevention trial in a screened military population, not a universal premarital population.
limits_of_this_search: This search covered 11 PubMed queries via NCBI E-utilities (esearch/esummary/efetch), reading full abstracts for 20 of the highest-relevance records out of ~70 unique PMIDs surfaced; it is not a systematic review and does not claim exhaustive coverage. Several broad terms ('coercive') returned substantial off-topic noise (psychiatric coercion, food-parenting-practice scales) that had to be filtered by title/abstract triage rather than retrieved directly. No non-PubMed-indexed grey literature, non-English-language Thai sources, or unpublished practice guidelines were searched, per the hard constraint to use PubMed-indexed literature and global-level guidance (WHO/UN/USPSTF/Cochrane) only; only one USPSTF-commissioned systematic review (Feltner 2018/JAMA) met the global-guidance tier in this angle. No record found or cited states or implies that T-PHE itself is effective; all findings are about the surrounding literature on couple-work safety, IPV typology, and coercive-control measurement/screening, offered as context for evaluating T-PHE's stop-rule and safeguard design, not as evidence of T-PHE's outcomes.
